title: What can help relieve anxiety before surgery
intro: Feeling nervous before an operation is very common. Anxiety can concern the anaesthetic, pain, the result or being away from home. Good information, preparation and simple relaxation techniques can reduce worry, and your care team can offer further support.

sections.heading: Why anxiety happens
paragraphs: Surgery involves unfamiliar places, loss of control and fear of the unknown. Past experiences, the type of operation and personal worries about illness or family can increase anxiety. High anxiety can raise heart rate and blood pressure, and some people find pain more difficult to bear, which is why it deserves attention.

sections.heading: Information and preparation
paragraphs: Ask your surgeon and anaesthetist exactly what will happen, how long it will take, what you will feel afterwards and when you can go home. Written material, videos or a tour of the ward can help. Writing down questions beforehand ensures nothing is forgotten. Knowing what to expect often reduces fear.

sections.heading: Relaxation and mind techniques
paragraphs: Slow breathing, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, listening to music and mindfulness have been shown to lower anxiety in many people. You can practise in the days before the operation and use headphones in the waiting area. Gentle exercise, good sleep and avoiding too much caffeine also help.

sections.heading: Medical help
paragraphs: If anxiety is severe, tell the team. Sometimes a mild calming medicine is offered before the operation, and the anaesthetist can explain the options. Talking therapy may help people with long-standing anxiety or strong fear of anaesthesia or needles. Do not take sleeping tablets or sedatives on your own before surgery without checking.

sections.heading: On the day
paragraphs: Bring something comforting, such as music or a book, and a trusted person if allowed. Tell staff that you feel nervous so that they can reassure you. Afterwards, discuss how it went and ask about pain relief, which also helps recovery.

examples.title: Practising breathing
examples.text: Imagine you feel tense the night before. You could breathe in slowly for four counts and out for six, repeating for several minutes.

examples.title: Asking questions
examples.text: Suppose you fear the anaesthetic. You might ask the anaesthetist how it works, how you will be monitored and what you will feel on waking.

questions: What exactly will happen before, during and after the operation?
Would a calming medicine or other support help me?
Can someone stay with me until I go to theatre?
